query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Wear resistance in high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by the mechanical-shear–induced formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or dynamic amorphous/nanocrystalline) surface layer during sliding. This layer enhances resistance to wear by combining high shear strength with the ability to deform homogeneously.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-sprayed or conventionally processed HEA coating with a relatively coarser-grained or mixed-phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled sliding wear tests that deliberately vary the applied shear stress (through different load levels) and environmental oxygen availability to either promote or suppress the dynamic transformation of the surface microstructure.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under inert or moderately oxidizing environments at loads sufficient to induce shear-driven microstructural transformation (within the regime where applied stress exceeds the threshold for dynamic amorphization), over a temperature range where these transformations are feasible.
generation.structural_mediator: The transition of the near-surface region into an ultra-nanocrystalline (or dynamically amorphous/nanocrystalline) layer, characterized by a high density of refined grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During sliding wear, mechanical shear (and, where present, reactive oxidation) triggers a dynamic refinement of the microstructure. The creation of the ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer increases resistance to further deformation and crack propagation, thereby lowering the friction coefficient and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that form the nano-scale transformed surface layer under sliding conditions will exhibit significantly lower friction and wear rates compared to a baseline coating where this transformation is absent or suppressed.
generation.baseline: Wear tests carried out under conditions that do not induce the dynamic transformation (e.g., lower loads, inert conditions that prevent either shear or oxide-driven transformation) will maintain the original coarser-grained microstructure, resulting in higher wear rates and friction.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should operate within the range of applied shear stresses and oxygen partial pressures that are sufficient to trigger the dynamic surface transformation. Extremely high or low oxygen environments, very low applied stresses, or conditions that do not allow for sufficient plastic deformation could fall outside this mechanism’s effective range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact balance between mechanical shear and reactive oxidation in facilitating the surface layer formation is not fully delineated in current studies, making it uncertain to attribute the wear performance solely to one of these effects under all conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA coatings and conduct sliding wear experiments under the same mechanical loading conditions. In one set, introduce a surface treatment (e.g., an alloying addition or coating) designed to inhibit the dynamic formation of a nanocrystalline layer. Characterize the surface microstructure (using TEM/SEM) and measure wear rates and friction coefficients for both sets.
measurements: Surface microstructure (TEM/SEM) to verify the presence or absence of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the treated samples (with inhibited dynamic surface transformation) show wear performance (i.e., friction and wear rates) that is statistically indistinguishable from that of the untreated samples, indicating that the formation of the nanocrystalline surface layer is not the governing factor in wear resistance.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces

Abstract: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. The reactive wear protection strategy offers a pathway for designing ultra-wear resistant alloys
